A new documentary titled "All of Us," now streaming on Apple TV, tells the story of a public elementary school that meets the educational needs of a remarkably diverse group of students in its own unique way.

Both iPhone and iPad have proven to be key tools in delivering what has been hailed as a model of inclusive education—one where every child benefits……

Students with special needs, who require additional support due to disabilities, have traditionally been taught separately from their peers. The conventional wisdom holds that placing everyone in the same classroom would be disruptive to the majority of students.

Ruby Bridges Elementary takes a fundamentally different view, and the results speak for themselves: rather than causing disruption, inclusive teaching has delivered significant academic and social benefits for all students. The outcomes have been so impressive that both the principal and a kindergarten teacher have been named Principal of the Year and Teacher of the Year for 2025.

A 70-minute documentary, now available on Apple TV, tells the story of "a school that breaks the mold."

At Ruby Bridges, every student learns together in a general education classroom. Every child does math together, reads together, and sings together in music class. Teachers and specialists work hand in hand in the classroom, and the results are plain to see. How do they do it? Ruby Bridges Elementary is a public school. Beyond the school's own resources, there is no extra funding, no extra staff, and no magic formula. There is simply a group of educators who decided to stop separating children and chose to put their faith in the power of learning together. This is the story of a school that breaks the mold—a school that is one of a kind, but really shouldn't have to be.

iPad and iPhone play a key role

Some students have severe communication difficulties, and augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) software running on iPad and iPhone has brought about a profound change in their ability to interact with teachers and fellow students.

An important finding is that AAC apps are not only useful for students with communication difficulties—they benefit every student equally. Founding principal Cathi Davis told me:

All students—whether they're high readers and strong language users, or just beginning to learn to communicate or use language—show remarkably high levels of engagement when they can use AAC tools to generate, expand, or express their ideas. With this always-available support for communication, we can work around all kinds of barriers—motor-skill challenges, limited writing stamina, anxiety about speaking up out loud—and at the same time break through the many barriers that come up in the classroom and in life……This is the very embodiment of what we mean by 'universal design.' Compared with just about every other language, communication, and vocabulary tool we use in the classroom, this one truly belongs to everyone.

As the documentary reveals, there's no question that this approach works for all students—not just those with additional needs. The documentary's official website also offers a rich library of video resources for other schools that wish to follow in Ruby Bridges' footsteps.
